description.narrative:
As outlined in the strategic direction 2025-2030 (Annex 1 A) the main mission for the ESCAP Multi-Donor Trust Fund for Tsunami, Disaster and Climate Preparedness (hereafter the ESCAP Tsunami TF) is "Implementation of people-centered, end-to-end multi hazards and interoperable early warning systems for transboundary coastal hazards"
In doing so, the ESCAP Tsunami TF will contribute towards "reducing the number of climate-related fatalities and affected populations and to reduced economic losses and damages attributed to disasters (Impact)".
Intermediary outcomes are 1) to increase national capacities which will enable effective utilization of early-warning systems (EWS) to generate and communicate actionable early warnings and 2) to share and implement innovative solutions for transboundary disaster risks and climate hazards across high-disaster risk, low-capacity countries.
The long-term outcomes are to empower local governments, communities, and critical sectors to take early action through enhanced disaster preparedness capacity and that the coverage of multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWS) is extended multi-dimensionally across a range of disasters and geographies and exposed populations.

Stöd till ESCAP:s givarfond för tsunami-, katastrof- och klimatberedskap och det strategiska ramverket för 2025–2030. Fondens mål är att "Öka införandet av heltäckande och kompatibla tidiga varningssystem med fokus på utsatta människor för olika typer av gränsöverskridande kustfaror". På så sätt kommer fonden att bidra till att "minska antalet klimatrelaterade dödsfall, drabbade befolkningar och bidra till minskade ekonomiska förluster och skador som kan tillskrivas katastrofer".

Support to the ESCAP Multi-Donor Trust Fund for Tsunami, Disaster and Climate Preparedness and its strategic direction 2025-2030. The main mission is "Implementation of people-centered, end-to-end multi hazards and interoperable early warning systems for transboundary coastal hazards". In doing so, the fund will contribute towards "reducing the number of climate-related fatalities and affected populations and to reduced economic losses and damages attributed to disasters ".

Impact of Swedish Support to the Tsunami Trust Fund (Summary of 20 years support - including renewed support 2024-2026)
Sweden's support has been pivotal in shaping the ESCAP Multi-Donor Trust Fund for Tsunami, Disaster and Climate Preparedness into a durable, high impact regional mechanism. Catalyst for a regionally owned financing model: As a founding donor in 2005, Sweden helped validate and de-risk a then-novel, regionally managed trust fund following the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami. This early leadership mobilized ten additional donors, unlocked sustained co-financing, and contributed to the Trust Fund becoming one of the few UN trust funds owned and managed at the regional level. Sustained, cost-effective resilience gains: With total contributions of USD 3.17 million, Sweden is now the Trust Funds second-largest contributor. Independent evaluations show strong returns, with every dollar invested generating USD 3.75.5 in economic and social benefits, and benefits outweighing costs within six years demonstrating effective translation of regional cooperation into real risk reduction.
Life-saving early warning systems and institutions: Swedish support enabled the establishment and strengthening of tsunami early warning systems across the Indian Ocean, including the IOTWMS, estimated to save around 1,000 lives per year over the next century. It also supported a shift toward multi-hazard preparedness, contributing to the creation and expansion of RIMES, now serving 62 countries and helping transform the region from reactive response to proactive resilience.
Inclusive, rights-based early action: Sweden's advocacy reinforced the integration of human rights, gender equality, and inclusion into early warning and preparedness efforts. This ensured systems better serve women, children, persons with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups, making resilience gains more equitable and sustainable.
Enduring regional relevance and demand: Strong interest in the Trust Fund evidenced by 161 proposals under the 20252026 call reflects its maturity and credibility. Sweden's long-term partnership has been central to sustaining this collective regional commitment to coastal resilience amid growing disaster and climate risks.
Overall, Swedish support has delivered outsized, lasting impact by strengthening regional cooperation, saving lives, building inclusive institutions, and anchoring a proven, scalable model for disaster and climate preparedness across Asia and the Pacific.
Specific results reported from 2025
Specific results reported from 2025 include that national and regional disaster risk reduction capacities have been measurably strengthened, resulting in more effective early warning systems (EWS) that generate and communicate actionable alerts while enabling timely early action. Through coordinated regional and subnational activities, awareness and technical expertise among both decision-makers and practitioners have increased, equipping institutions with the mandates, tools, and preparedness resources needed to respond proactively particularly at the local level, where inclusive community preparedness and tsunami anticipatory action protocols have improved. Practical impact is evident in the translation of key resources into Farsi and Urdu and the successful participation of five countries in the Indian Ocean Wave 2025 exercise, demonstrating inclusive approaches that meaningfully engage at-risk populations. At the same time, strengthened transboundary early warning systems (IOTWMS and PTWS) and expanded knowledge-sharing have enhanced cooperation across high-risk, low-capacity countries, with ESCAP and non-ESCAP members actively applying preparedness assessment findings. These combined efforts have extended multi-hazard early warning coverage across diverse geographies, indirectly reaching over 19 million people in pilot cities, while also building individual and institutional capacity through regional training involving participants from 17 countries.
